questions.q: What conceptual shape do cursors share across all four platforms, even though the syntax differs?
options: There is no shared concept — each platform's cursor works completely differently
Declare the cursor, open it, fetch rows in a loop, then close it when done
Only SELECT statements can be used, never INSERT or UPDATE, on any platform
Cursors always return exactly one row on every platform
questions.explain: DECLARE/OPEN/FETCH-loop/CLOSE is the shared conceptual shape, even though T-SQL, PL/SQL, MySQL, and PostgreSQL each spell the steps differently.

questions.q: What two FETCH calls does a T-SQL cursor loop require, and why?
options: One FETCH NEXT before the loop starts (to prime @@FETCH_STATUS) and another at the bottom of the loop body
FETCH is not used in T-SQL cursors at all
T-SQL only ever needs a single FETCH statement
T-SQL requires three FETCH calls per loop iteration
questions.explain: Missing either the priming FETCH NEXT before the WHILE loop or the one inside the loop body causes the loop to never run or never end.

questions.q: What is the 'nicer ergonomics' this lesson highlights about PL/SQL's cursor-FOR-loop compared to its explicit cursor syntax?
options: It cannot be used with a WHERE clause
It is the only way to use a cursor in PL/SQL at all
It automatically handles OPEN, FETCH, and CLOSE, with no manual bookkeeping needed
It requires MORE manual steps than the explicit cursor
questions.explain: FOR rec IN (SELECT...) LOOP...END LOOP; opens the cursor, fetches every row, and closes it automatically — unlike the explicit CURSOR/OPEN/FETCH/EXIT WHEN/CLOSE form.

questions.q: How does MySQL detect that a cursor has run out of rows inside a stored program?
options: MySQL automatically exits the loop with no handler needed
MySQL uses the same @@FETCH_STATUS variable as T-SQL
A declared CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND sets a flag variable, which the loop checks to decide when to LEAVE
MySQL cursors cannot detect the end of a result set
questions.explain: MySQL has no %NOTFOUND or @@FETCH_STATUS equivalent — instead, a DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND sets a flag variable when FETCH finds no more rows.

questions.q: Which platform supports a FOR rec IN SELECT...LOOP...END LOOP idiom nearly identical to Oracle's cursor-FOR-loop?
options: MySQL
PostgreSQL's PL/pgSQL
None of the other three platforms support this idiom
T-SQL
questions.explain: PL/pgSQL supports the same FOR rec IN SELECT...LOOP...END LOOP idiom as Oracle's PL/SQL, and it's the idiomatic way to iterate on PostgreSQL too.
